chapter_title: A Friend Found in Music (Twin Melodies)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 50 minutes × 5 periods = 250 minutes
Total: 5 periods · 4h 10min

periods.activity_title: Reading the Poem and Exploring Its Core Metaphors

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.194): share personal music preferences, favourite musicians, and reasons.
Reflect and Respond (p.195): complete the poet’s diary by filling eight blanks from the poem.

time_bands.activity: Teacher-led warm-up: students share briefly which kind of music they prefer and name a favourite musician, giving a reason. Responses are taken from three or four volunteers to open the emotional register of the poem.

Unhurried read-aloud of the full poem (p.194–195), teacher reading once with expression, then students reading chorally. Attention is drawn to the anaphoric ‘Music is…’ pattern and the ABCB rhyme as audible features.

Students work individually to complete the poet’s diary activity from Reflect and Respond (p.195), filling all eight blanks using words from the poem. Pairs compare and justify their choices before a brief whole-class check.
Teacher draws out which stanza each diary entry matches, showing how the poem’s structure maps onto the speaker’s emotional arc from longing to gratitude.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens with the poem itself, so the read-aloud is the gateway to all later work; pace it generously so the anaphora lands. The diary-fill task requires students to track exact words from the poem, which trains close attention before metaphor analysis begins. Students sometimes confuse ‘pull through’ as a simple movement phrase; note the phrasal-verb dimension for the vocabulary unit that builds on this poem.

periods.activity_title: Appreciating Poetic Devices and the Poem’s Deeper Meaning

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Appreciation (p.195): identify polysemy, convert metaphors to similes, analyse rhyme scheme, anaphora, and message.

homework.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.196): answer all five sub-questions on the therapy-and-spirits extract independently.

time_bands.activity: Quick re-reading of the poem (p.194–195) aloud by student volunteers, one stanza each, to reactivate the text. Teacher prompts students to listen for the phrase ‘moves me’ and note its double sense before analysis begins.

Paired close-reading of the Reading for Appreciation questions (p.195): students identify the polysemy in ‘moves me,’ list all four metaphors, and rewrite each as a simile. Pairs share their simile conversions and the class evaluates which simile best preserves the emotional weight.

Whole-class discussion of rhyme scheme, the purpose of anaphoric repetition, and the poem’s central message. Teacher models identifying ABCB on the board using stanza one, then students verify stanzas two and three independently before sharing.
Students write a two-sentence personal response: which metaphor they find most powerful and why. Two or three are shared aloud; teacher notes the range of choices to affirm multiple valid readings.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem aloud and completed the diary activity, students now look beneath surface meaning; steer them away from paraphrase toward device identification. A common difficulty is distinguishing a metaphor from a simile in reverse — remind students a simile must carry ‘as…as’ or ‘like,’ and the metaphor they convert must retain the same emotional comparison. The mood-identification sub-question (MCQ type in the appreciation set) is deliberately left for the self-study note below: students may attempt it as consolidation after the discussion.

periods.activity_title: Listening to a Santoor Dilemma, Then Role-Playing Music’s Benefits

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.199): predict answers to six questions before listening, then verify after hearing the conversation.
Speaking Activity (p.199–200): four-role group role play — music teacher, two students, parent — on whether music classes are worthwhile.

time_bands.activity: Students read the six Listen and Respond questions silently (p.199) and write their predicted answers. Brief pair discussion of predictions before listening to set purpose and activate schema about music learning contexts.

Teacher reads the transcript aloud (or plays a recorded version) of the mother-and-Jaspreet conversation about the santoor. Students check and correct their predicted answers, then discuss with the class which prediction was hardest to make and why.

Groups of four prepare and perform the role play (p.199–200): music teacher, Student 1 (time-worried), Student 2 (convinced learner), and Parent (initially doubtful). Each group uses the cue roles to build a logical conversation; teacher circulates and prompts with a question if a group stalls.

Two groups share their role plays briefly. Class notes one strong argument used by each group for the benefit of music study, connecting the discussion back to the poem’s portrayal of music as emotional sustenance.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening transcript features the santoor — a plucked string instrument — and students who are unfamiliar with it may guess wrongly between sitar, sarod, and santoor; a one-line description at prediction time helps without spoiling the answer. The role play should move toward genuine argument with reasons, not just scripted turns; prompt Student 1 and Parent roles to push back so Student 2 and the music teacher must reason, not just assert. The Check Your Understanding and Answer the Following questions from the Reading for Comprehension spine are not anchored this unit; flag them to students as worthwhile self-study to deepen their reading of the poem.
materials: Transcript text (Unit 6, p.270 of the transcript appendix) for teacher reference

periods.activity_title: Phrasal Verbs in Context and Drafting an Invitation Letter

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary in Context (p.197): classify emotion words and select correct vocabulary items from bracketed pairs.
Vocabulary in Context (p.198): match six ‘move’ phrasal verbs to their meanings from the given box.
Writing Task (p.200–201): draft a personalised invitation letter to grandparents for a World Music Day sitar recital.

time_bands.activity: Vocabulary work (p.197): teacher leads classification of ‘feel blue / lifts my spirits / most cheerful’ into positive and negative emotion columns, then students complete the four bracketed-choice sentences. Whole-class check focuses on register distinctions (e.g. ‘melancholy’ vs ‘despair’) and how context in a music piece signals the right word.

Phrasal verb matching (p.198): students work individually to match the six ‘move’-based phrasal verbs to meanings from the box, then compare with a partner. Teacher confirms answers and highlights how the preposition changes meaning entirely, connecting to ‘pull through’ from the poem.

Guided writing of the invitation letter (p.200–201): teacher displays the required format on the board (address, date, salutation, body, close) and students draft their own letter in full, using first-person ‘I’ and a warm, personalised tone. Pairs swap for a quick peer read to check format completeness and tone before the unit ends.
Teacher draws attention to one strong example of warm tone from a volunteer’s letter and one common format error to consolidate the functional writing register.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit keeps vocabulary_grammar in its own block before moving to writing, as required. Students frequently confuse ‘jubilant’ and ‘euphoric’ as interchangeable; the context clue (‘festive symphony / joyous occasion’) is the anchor for the correct choice. The invitation letter requires a genuinely personalised, affectionate register — discourage formal office-letter openings and remind students the recipient is a grandparent. The phrasal-verb creation task (task index 3 in the vocabulary spine) is not anchored here; students may explore it independently as an enrichment activity.

periods.activity_title: Music as Heritage, Therapy, and Universal Voice — Chapter Synthesis

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.201): research and discuss music as alternative therapy, linking Raga Chikitsa and Sangita Sudha to present-day practice.
Learning Beyond the Text (p.201): share poems and songs about music from English and other languages and begin a class collection.
Check Your Understanding (p.196): answer analytical questions on music moving the poet, the ‘needed friend’ comparison, the poet’s attitude, universal appeal, and personal response.

time_bands.activity: Brief whole-class discussion on Raga Chikitsa and Sangita Sudha (p.201): teacher introduces the idea that Indian classical tradition has long recognised music’s healing role, and students share any knowledge of music therapy they have encountered. The discussion anchors the poem’s therapy metaphor in a real cultural-heritage tradition.

Students share a poem, song, or lyric about music they know — in English or any other language — and the class begins building a collective list on the board. Each entry is tagged with its language and the emotion it expresses, creating a multilingual record of music’s universal resonance.

Critical reading of the poem in light of the full chapter: students work in pairs to answer two of the five Check Your Understanding questions (p.196) — focusing on the poet’s attitude and the poem’s universal appeal — and then share reasoning aloud. Teacher steers responses toward textual evidence, asking students to name the specific metaphor or line that supports their claim.

Synthesis close: teacher invites one student to name the single metaphor from the poem that best captures music’s role as described across the chapter — as emotional therapy, cultural heritage, and unwavering companion. Class votes and the reasoning is noted, ending with the poem’s own final lines read aloud together.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through the poem’s devices, the listening dilemma about santoor practice, the role play on music’s value, and the invitation letter, students now stand back and see the chapter’s full arc: music as personal therapy, cultural heritage, and universal companion. The Check Your Understanding questions on universal appeal and the poet’s attitude are the analytical crux of this synthesis; push students to cite a metaphor as evidence rather than paraphrase the theme. The Walter de la Mare poem noted under Learning Beyond the Text is a self-directed reading pleasure piece and carries no exercise apparatus; point students to it as an extension for personal enjoyment.
materials: Whiteboard for multilingual song/poem collection list

items.source_lo: Student analyses poetic devices, tone, and authorial purpose using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Bryanna T. Perkins’s use of anaphora, metaphor, rhyme scheme, and the music-as-companion theme.
items.item_stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of beginning each new idea with the words ‘Music is…’ throughout the poem?

options.label: A
options.text: It creates a meditative, incantatory rhythm that reinforces music’s constant presence in the speaker’s life.

options.label: B
options.text: It shows the speaker is unable to think of other ways to begin a sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: It signals that each stanza describes a completely different speaker with a different relationship to music.

options.label: D
options.text: It emphasises that music is only important during moments of sadness.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student recognises repetition but misreads it as stylistic limitation rather than a deliberate device.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student misunderstands anaphora as a structural marker of different speakers rather than a unifying refrain.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has focused only on the second stanza’s sad-mood reference and missed the poem’s full emotional arc.

items.source_lo: Student analyses poetic devices, tone, and authorial purpose using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Bryanna T. Perkins’s use of anaphora, metaphor, rhyme scheme, and the music-as-companion theme.
items.item_stem:
Read the second stanza on p.195, beginning “Music is the therapy.”

(i) What two emotional states does the speaker describe in this stanza, and how does music respond to each?
(ii) The poem’s appreciation summary calls the tone ‘warmly affirmative.’ Evaluate how far this stanza supports that description, citing the specific words that most clearly carry the tone.
items.visual_stimulus: Read the second stanza on p.195, beginning “Music is the therapy.”

expected_elements: Names sadness (‘feel blue’) and the need to recover (‘pull through’) as the two states.
Identifies ‘lifts my spirits’ as music’s active, positive response to sadness.
Explains ‘warmly affirmative’ as confidence that music will help, not merely hope.
Cites ‘to make sure’ as the phrase that carries certainty and warmth simultaneously.
Acknowledges the stanza begins in distress but ends on assured resilience.

items.source_lo: Student listens purposefully to a spoken conversation, predicts outcomes, and verifies comprehension using a listening text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Jaspreet’s santoor-practice problem and his mother’s solution of borrowing an instrument from a friend.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the conversation between Jaspreet and his mother. Then select the correct answer for each question.

Statements:
1. Jaspreet is upset because his santoor teacher comes to the music centre only twice a week.
2. Jaspreet tried watching videos of the santoor being played and found it very helpful.
3. Jaspreet’s mother resolves the problem by offering to borrow a santoor from her friend.

options.text: Jaspreet is upset because his santoor teacher comes to the music centre only twice a week.
Jaspreet tried watching videos of the santoor being played and found it very helpful.
Jaspreet’s mother resolves the problem by offering to borrow a santoor from her friend.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. True — the transcript states the teacher comes only twice a week, making regular practice difficult. 2. False — Jaspreet explains he tried watching videos but it did not help because playing is a hands-on skill. 3. True — his mother says she has a friend who used to play the santoor and can lend the instrument.

items.source_lo: Student listens purposefully to a spoken conversation, predicts outcomes, and verifies comprehension using a listening text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Jaspreet’s santoor-practice problem and his mother’s solution of borrowing an instrument from a friend.
items.item_stem: After hearing the conversation, explain in two or three sentences why Jaspreet rejected watching videos as a solution to his practice problem, and what this tells us about the nature of learning a musical instrument.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Jaspreet rejected watching videos because playing an instrument is a hands-on skill that cannot be learned through observation alone. This reveals that musical learning requires physical practice with the instrument, not just intellectual or visual understanding.

items.source_lo: Student argues a position with rationale and responds to opposing views using a structured role play as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Four-role debate on whether music classes are beneficial despite pressure on study time.
items.item_stem: You are a student who learns a musical instrument. A classmate argues that music classes waste time that should go to academic subjects. Describe clearly, in a one-minute spoken response, one specific reason why you believe music study is compatible with academic success. Use a concrete example from your own experience or from something you have heard or read.

expected_elements: States one clear, reasoned claim about music and academic compatibility.
Supports the claim with a concrete example, not a general assertion.
Directly acknowledges and responds to the classmate’s concern about time.
Maintains a confident, coherent spoken delivery throughout.
Uses appropriate vocabulary relating to music or learning context.

items.source_lo: Student argues a position with rationale and responds to opposing views using a structured role play as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Four-role debate on whether music classes are beneficial despite pressure on study time.
items.item_stem: Take the position of a parent who was initially doubtful about allowing a child to join music classes but has now been persuaded. In a two-minute spoken argument, explain what changed your mind, anticipate at least one counter-argument from someone still unconvinced, and respond to it with a reason grounded in the value of music as a companion and emotional support.

expected_elements: Clearly names what persuaded the parent, linked to music’s emotional or well-being value.
Articulates at least one genuine counter-argument a sceptic would raise.
Responds to the counter-argument with a specific reason, not a dismissal.
Maintains the parent’s shifted perspective consistently throughout.
Uses persuasive register with appropriate hedging and assertion.

items.item_stem: Your school is hosting an intercultural art exhibition where students present work inspired by music, poetry, and dance traditions from across India. Write a notice for your school noticeboard informing students of the exhibition’s date, venue, and how they can contribute an entry. Your notice should be clear, formal in register, and include all essential details a student would need.

expected_elements: Uses correct notice format: heading, date, body, name/designation of issuer.
Includes event details: purpose, date, venue, and how to participate.

items.item_stem: A local newspaper has published an opinion piece arguing that arts subjects such as music and poetry should be reduced in school timetables to give more time to science and mathematics. Write a letter to the editor responding to this view. In your letter, argue for the importance of arts in students’ emotional and intellectual development, using at least one specific reason and one concrete example.

expected_elements: Uses correct letter-to-editor format: date, addressee, salutation, body, sign-off.
States a clear counter-position to the newspaper’s opinion in the opening paragraph.

Maintains a formal, respectful but assertive argumentative register throughout.
Closes with a call to action or a summary of the position argued.

items.source_lo: Student identifies and uses phrasal verbs and emotion-register vocabulary in context using the poem’s language as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Emotion words (feel blue, lifts my spirits, most cheerful) and ‘move’-based phrasal verbs from the poem.
items.item_stem: Match each emotion word or phrase in Column A with its correct meaning in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Column A | Column B |
|---|---|
| feel blue | to feel very happy and full of energy |
| lifts my spirits | to feel sad or unhappy |
| most cheerful | makes one feel more positive and hopeful |
| euphoric | in the happiest or most positive state |
| melancholy | a deep, gentle sadness |

answer_key.right: makes one feel more positive and hopeful
in the happiest or most positive state
to feel very happy and full of energy

items.source_lo: Student identifies and uses phrasal verbs and emotion-register vocabulary in context using the poem’s language as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Emotion words (feel blue, lifts my spirits, most cheerful) and ‘move’-based phrasal verbs from the poem.
items.item_stem:
The poem uses the phrasal verb ‘pull through’ to mean ‘to succeed despite difficulty.’ The verb ‘move’ similarly forms several phrasal verbs by pairing with different prepositions. Rewrite each sentence below by replacing the underlined phrasal verb with its correct meaning, chosen from the list in the box: (leave a place permanently / progress to a new stage / shift to create space / begin to move away / start living in a new home)

1. After years in one neighbourhood, the family finally decided to move on.
2. The removal van moved off once the last box was loaded.
3. Could you move over so that your younger sister can sit beside you?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. ‘move on’ = progress to a new stage (or leave a place/situation permanently, depending on context). 2. ‘moved off’ = begin to move away. 3. ‘move over’ = shift to create space.

items.source_lo: Student explores cultural heritage and cross-linguistic connections using interdisciplinary research as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Indian classical music’s healing tradition (Raga Chikitsa, Sangita Sudha) and music therapy in present-day times.
items.item_stem: The poem describes music as ‘the therapy I need when I feel blue.’ In a short paragraph of four to five sentences, explain what you know or have found out about how music has been used for healing in India’s classical tradition. Name at least one historical text or tradition, and connect it to one way music therapy is practised today.

expected_elements: Names at least one classical Indian text or tradition (e.g. Raga Chikitsa or Sangita Sudha).
Explains briefly what that text or tradition says about music and healing or emotions.
Makes a clear connection between the historical tradition and a present-day practice.
Links the discussion back to the poem’s therapy metaphor in at least one sentence.
Written in coherent prose with a clear organisational logic.

items.source_lo: Student explores cultural heritage and cross-linguistic connections using interdisciplinary research as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Indian classical music’s healing tradition (Raga Chikitsa, Sangita Sudha) and music therapy in present-day times.
items.item_stem: Create a short annotated collection of three poems or songs about music — at least one in English and at least one in another Indian language you know or have access to. For each entry write: (a) the title and poet/composer, (b) the language it is written in, and (c) one sentence describing the emotion or idea about music it expresses. Then write a brief comparative note (three to four sentences) on what all three entries suggest about music’s role across languages and cultures.

expected_elements: Includes at least one English and one other Indian language entry, each correctly attributed.
Each annotation names a specific emotion or idea, not a vague summary.
The comparative note identifies a shared theme or contrast across the three entries.
Shows awareness that music’s emotional resonance is cross-cultural and multilingual.
Collection is organised clearly so a reader can follow the three entries and the note.
